title: Majestic
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later boards reviewed. Begin after ...Qc2 at 114 seconds in the complete eight-piece later diagram. Be6 is certified against every legal Black reply: actual mates or legal captures reaching exact supported seven-piece wins. The source Qc4/b3+/Qxb3/Bxb3 mate and b4/Bd7+/Qc6/Bxc6 mate are encoded; three queen alternatives are independently labeled. Earlier Qd1 sacrifice, queen-capture and Ka2/Qa1 stalemate comparisons remain unverified context outside this selected root. Captures retain the remaining pawns; no material-only or larger-engine estimate substitutes for proof.
transcript: Black's brilliant idea is bishop to b1 check, sacrificing the bishop completely. But once the bishop is taken, black follows up with queen to f1 check. And if white is not careful and simply tries to escape the check with king to a2, this is going to be followed up by queen to a1, giving up the last of the black pieces for a stalemate. The black king and the pawns have no legal moves since this pawn is pinned to the king, so this would be a draw. So white cannot hide in the corner with king [music] to a2. And believe it or not, the only way to keep this game going is a counter brilliancy. The incredible queen to d1. A move that doesn't even begin to make sense. Yes, this puts the queen in the way of the check, but the queen can simply be taken with another check. But white actually has made a small achievement. He can now safely play king to a2 because if the queen is sacrificed, this time there is not going to be a stalemate. Black still has legal moves available, and this would be winning for white. Not only queen to a1 doesn't work anymore, black has to be careful because there are two different checkmate threats. If the queen plays a random move, either pawn to b3 or bishop to b3 would both lead to a checkmate. So black needs to play a move that stops both of those threats, and he does that with queen to c2, defending b3 by the attack of the bishop and pinning the pawn to the king so that it cannot move. Now it seems like black has completely neutralized the threats of white and he's just going to have a queen for a bishop and simply win this game. For example, a random move like bishop to d5 would allow b4. And now there is a threat of marching this pawn down the board and for example checkmate white like this. So is this it? Is black simply out of the woods in this position? Well, not exactly. You see, white had foreseen all of this when he decided to sacrifice his queen and he finds the incredibly precise only move bishop to e6 because indeed black is in zugzwang a situation where the best move would be to not move anything at all. Moving the b4 pawn now would allow bishop to d7 since the king is covering b3 black would be forced to give up the queen and get checkmated like this. And if the black queen moves pretty much anywhere she's just going to stop defending the threat of bishop to b3 checkmate. But black has one last ace up his sleeve queen to c4. Realizing that he cannot win this game he gives up the queen interjecting the bishop and hoping for this drawn end game but this is of no use because after queen to c4 white can just play pawn to b3 check almost checkmating black forcing queen takes b3 and bishop takes b3 checkmate.
